January 2027 planning  |  Prepared November 2026

slides.title: Launch Dispatch Copilot in a new Pro tier at +$12 per seat in Q4 2027, not as a $149 add-on in Q2: it is a ~$2M ARR expansion lever, and the mobile rewrite should go first

paragraphs.text: Launch Dispatch Copilot in a new Pro tier at +$12 per seat in Q4 2027, not as a $149 add-on in Q2: it is a ~$2M ARR expansion lever, and the mobile rewrite should go first
Copilot is worth launching, but it is worth ~$2M of ARR, not $8M

The $8M rests on a survey with a 6% response rate; only 14% of engaged beta accounts actually paid $149. Realistic new ARR is $1.2–2.9M. It is still the only lever in the pack that adds the expansion NRR needs: without it NRR reaches ~103%, short of 105%.
Package it in Pro at +$12 per seat with a usage allowance, not as a $149 add-on

A flat per-account fee draws the heaviest users (buyers average 6,800 requests, $61 a month of inference) and is an extra charge where Routewise includes AI in Pro. Pro base case: $2.2M ARR, $0.9M gross profit, 76.6% company margin. Free inclusion would cut margin to 70–74%.
Launch in Q4 2027 and keep the mobile rewrite on schedule

Mobile reliability causes 27% of churn, AI 6%. A two-quarter mobile delay loses ~$0.54M of ARR for good; a two-quarter Copilot delay loses ~$0.28M and defers ~$0.4M of profit. The money is close, so the stronger evidence and longer-lasting effect of the mobile fix decide it.
Use 2027 to prove Copilot with non-volunteers, with a trigger to launch sooner

Run a randomised Pro pilot, keep beta accounts live, equip Sales for Routewise deals and renegotiate inference before Dec 2027. Bring launch forward to Q2 only if the Q4 2026 data show AI, not Routewise's 20% discount, drove the lost deals and the rewrite will fix <40% of mobile churn.
Source: Brightwork briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis. Ranges show low–high cases; base case in bold. ARR = annual recurring revenue; NRR = net revenue retention.

slides.title: The $8M forecast assumes 46% of accounts will buy; actual buying behaviour points to $1.2–2.5M of new ARR for a $149 add-on

The $8M forecast assumes 46% of accounts will buy; actual buying behaviour points to $1.2–2.5M of new ARR for a $149 add-on
New ARR from a $149/account/month add-on, $M
Why the survey overstates demand ~3–6×
Self-selected sample. Only 610 of 9,800 admins replied (6%). People who reply to an AI survey tend to be the ones interested in AI.
Skewed to large accounts. Respondents average 9.4 seats vs 6.2 across the base.
Intent is not purchase. 'Likely' or 'very likely' (46%) compares with the 14% of beta accounts that paid after 8+ weeks of free use: 3.3× lower.
Even 14% is a ceiling. Beta accounts volunteered, are larger (8.1 seats) and more active than the base. The typical account is likely to buy at a lower rate.
Implication: plan on $1.2–2.5M for the add-on. That is enough to matter for NRR (+2–4 pts) but it is not an $8M business.
How it is calculated: accounts × buy rate × $149 × 12

Source: Brightwork briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis. §4, §6, §10. Low case assumes non-volunteer accounts buy at half the volunteer rate (our assumption). Survey n = 610 of 9,800 admins.

slides.title: Beta gains are encouraging, but they come from volunteers, so the productivity case is unproven for the typical customer

Beta gains are encouraging, but they come from volunteers, so the productivity case is unproven for the typical customer
Beta (240 volunteer accounts) vs matched non-beta accounts
Why the gains may not carry over to the whole base
Selection bias. Volunteers chose to join; they are larger (8.1 vs 6.2 seats) and more active. Engaged accounts renew more anyway.
Concentrated use. The median account sent 1,900 requests a month, the mean 3,600 and the top 10% 14,500*. A few power users drive the averages.
Short window. 12 weeks, with novelty effects, and a 90-day renewal read on a sample of 240.
Still a real signal. A 9-point productivity gap against a matched group is not nothing. It needs confirming, not dismissing.
Change in jobs scheduled per dispatcher-hour vs prior 12 weeks
90-day renewal rate
Implication: run a randomised pilot on non-volunteer accounts (slide 14) before committing to scale assumptions. Our Pro base case already discounts the beta results.
Dispatchers also self-reported 4.1 hours saved per week (no control group, so not measured).

Source: Brightwork briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis. §5 Tables 1–2. *Table 2 implies the top 10% generate ~40% of requests (14,500 × 10% ÷ 3,600), not the 58% stated; either way usage is concentrated.

NRR bridge to 2028 vs the 105% target, base case, % (levers at full effect)
Can each lever reach 105% on its own?
Only Copilot can reach 105% alone, and only in the base case. Both levers together give a margin of safety.
Migration is a one-off step. NRR rises while accounts move to Pro, then the uplift fades; lower churn from a reliable app keeps paying every year.
So the question is not whether to do Copilot, but in what order: section 3.
Axis starts at 100% (no net change). Target: 105%. Orange marks the non-Copilot lever.

Source: Brightwork briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis. §3, §8. Lever size = ARR effect ÷ $57.6M. Pro: 25% of accounts × 6.2 seats × $12 × 12. Mobile: 50% of the 27% mobile-driven churn removed (assumption). AI churn: half of 6% AI-driven churn avoided (assumption).

The competitive threat is real but worth at most ~$0.6M of new ARR a year, not the ~$1.9M the Sales memo implies
Win rate where Routewise competes
Why the true AI effect is likely smaller
Confounded timing. In the same quarter, Routewise offered 20% off the first year. The drop may be about price, not AI.
Mention is not cause. 31% of loss notes mention AI; that does not mean AI decided those deals.
Testable now. The promo ran in Q3 2026. If the Q4 2026 win rate recovers towards 44%, AI was not the main driver.
Doesn't count towards NRR. New-logo wins grow ARR but are outside the NRR objective.

Sales memo: a third of 983 lost deals = 328 deals = $1.93M. That needs a 58% win rate, well above the 44% before Routewise launched AI.
Implication: competing means matching Routewise's packaging (AI in Pro) as much as the feature. The base case assumes AI explains half the drop: ~$0.32M ARR a year.
Source: Brightwork briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis. §7, §10, §11. ARR per new account = 6.2 seats × $79 × 12 = $5,878. Contested opportunities = 2,600 × 60% = 1,560 a year.

slides.title: A flat $149 fee attracts heavy users whose inference cost nearly eats the price; per-seat pricing with an allowance keeps cost in step with revenue

A flat $149 fee attracts heavy users whose inference cost nearly eats the price; per-seat pricing with an allowance keeps cost in step with revenue
Monthly inference cost per account vs the $149 add-on price
Per seat: revenue scales with account size
Seats track use: beta accounts were 8.1 seats and used 444 requests per seat.
Without a cap, a heavy-user Pro mix breaks the margin rule: company margin 74.1–74.8% at 25–33% adoption. With a 500-request allowance it stays at 76.3–76.4%.
Those who buy are the heavy users: buyers averaged 6,800 requests a month, nearly twice the beta mean.
Price is the same for every account, but cost grows with use, so the best customers are the least profitable.
Implication: price per seat and include a pooled usage allowance; sell extra usage in packs rather than giving it away.

Source: Brightwork briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis. §5 Table 2, §6. Inference at $0.009 per request (fixed through Dec 2027). Per-seat use = beta mean 3,600 ÷ 8.1 seats = 444 requests. Heavy case = Pro adopters behave like paywall buyers (6,800 per 6.2-seat account).

slides.title: Delaying the mobile rewrite costs about twice as much lasting ARR as delaying Copilot, so the rewrite should go first

Delaying the mobile rewrite costs about twice as much lasting ARR as delaying Copilot, so the rewrite should go first
Cost of a two-quarter delay, base case, $M
The money is close; three tie-breakers favour mobile

categories: Delay mobile: ARR lost for good
Delay Copilot: ARR lost for good

paragraphs.text: Evidence quality. Mobile's cost comes from real churn data. Copilot's comes from volunteers and a win-rate drop that coincides with a price promotion.
Durability. Lower churn is a lasting gain. Deferring Copilot only moves profit later, and once the accounts have migrated to Pro, NRR is the same.
Fit with the 2028 target. A Q4 2027 launch puts ~75% of a 12-month Pro migration inside 2028, against ~25% for a Q2 launch (if NRR is measured on calendar 2028).
Implication: keep the rewrite on schedule and launch Copilot two quarters later, in Q4 2027.
Mobile: ½ year × 50% × $2.18M mobile-driven churn = $0.54M
Copilot: ½ year × (50% × $0.64M win-rate recovery + 50% × $0.48M AI churn) = $0.28M
Deferred: ½ year × Pro gross profit $1.46M before platform, less $0.30M platform cost saved = $0.43M

Source: Brightwork briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis. §3, §7, §8. Assumes the constraint is a straight swap: whichever ships first delays the other by two quarters. Base: rewrite removes 50% of mobile churn (25–75%); AI explains 50% of the win-rate drop (0–100%); Copilot avoids 50% of AI churn.

Lasting-ARR advantage of mobile-first, $M
Trigger to bring the launch forward to end-Q2 2027

data: Share of mobile churn the rewrite removes ↓   /   share of the win-rate drop AI explains →

paragraphs.text: Bring the launch forward only if both are true at a trigger check by mid-February, once Q4 2026 data are final:
AI drove the lost deals: the Q4 2026 win rate vs Routewise stays at ~37% after the 20% promotion ended, and the share of loss notes citing AI rises.
The rewrite will under-deliver: Engineering and CS cannot show it removes at least ~40% of mobile-driven churn.
Otherwise hold Q4 2027. If the win rate recovers towards 44%, the case for waiting gets stronger: the Q3 drop was most likely the promotion, not AI.
Break-even: if AI explains 100% of the drop, mobile first needs the rewrite to remove ≥40% of mobile churn; at 50%, ≥26%.
Blue = mobile first is better; grey = neutral; red = Copilot first is better.

Source: Brightwork briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis. Cell = lasting ARR lost by delaying mobile two quarters, minus lasting ARR lost by delaying Copilot two quarters ($M). Positive = mobile first is better. Excludes the one-off $0.43M profit deferral, which favours Copilot first.

slides.title: Three decisions today lock in the plan and keep the option to launch sooner if the evidence shifts

paragraphs.text: 1  Is it worth launching?
2  How to package and price
3  When to launch
4  Making it work
Three decisions today lock in the plan and keep the option to launch sooner if the evidence shifts
Approve packaging and price
Copilot only inside a new Pro tier at $91 per seat (+$12), with 500 pooled AI requests per seat and paid packs above that. Do not launch the $149 add-on; do not include Copilot free in Core.
Approve the sequence
The mobile rewrite stays on schedule. Copilot GA targets late Q4 2027, with the 14-engineer build in H2. Engineering confirms by 31 January that the rewrite needs those engineers only in H1.
Approve the 2027 validation plan and trigger

Randomised Pro pilot on ~500 non-volunteer accounts; keep the beta accounts live (~$8k a month); renegotiate inference before Dec 2027; trigger check by mid-February using final Q4 2026 win-rate data.
What success looks like

By end-2028: 14–33% of accounts on Pro (base 25%, +$2.2M ARR), mobile-driven churn down by half (+$1.1M ARR kept a year), company gross margin ≥76%, and NRR at ~107% in the base case (104% in the low case, against a 105% target).
Source: Brightwork briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis.
